title: Unsupervised Learning
body:
Learning from data with **no labels**. There is no $y$, so there is no right answer to predict and
no way to score a prediction. What is left is the structure of the data itself.

**The absence of labels changes the question, not just the difficulty.** [[Supervised Learning]]
asks "what is the answer for this input"; this asks "what is going on in here", and that is a
question with no unique correct response. Two analysts can produce different groupings of the same
data and both be defensible.

## What it is used for

| Task | Question | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **[[Clustering]]** | which points belong together | [[Clustering]] |
| **Dimensionality reduction** | which directions carry the variation | [[Principal Component Analysis]] |
| **Anomaly detection** | which points belong to nothing | below |
| **Density estimation** | where is the data concentrated | no note |

**Anomaly detection** is the one with the most direct payoff and it is mostly clustering read
backwards: fit a notion of normal, then flag whatever sits far from it. Fraud detection, intrusion
detection, and failing-sensor detection are all this. It inherits one hard property: **anomalies
are rare by definition**, so the classes are wildly imbalanced and accuracy is a meaningless
score. [[Confusion Matrix]], [[Sensitivity]], and [[Specificity]] are the right instruments, and
[[Stratification]] is why naive sampling misleads. A detector that flags nothing is 99.9% accurate.

## Why evaluation is the hard part

With labels you hold out a test set and count. Without them there is nothing to count against, so
evaluation falls back to internal measures (are clusters tight and well separated), stability
(does the answer survive resampling), and whether a human finds the result useful. **None of these
is ground truth**, and treating an internal score as if it were is the standard mistake.

The practical consequence: unsupervised results are usually a *step*, not an answer. Cluster the
customers, then a person names the clusters and decides what to do. Reduce the dimensions, then
run [[Supervised Learning]] on the result.

Its real advantage is supply. Labelled data is expensive and unlabelled data is nearly free, which
is why the idea keeps coming back in stronger forms: modern self-supervised methods invent their
own labels from unlabelled data (hide part of the input, predict it), and that is what large
models are trained on. Not on this course, and worth knowing the lineage.
